title: Statistical Models of Top-k Partial Orders with Variable k

problem.claim: Ranked-preference data often consists of partial orders over alternatives, whose list lengths also need to be modeled.

gap.claim: Treating partial orders only as marginals of total orders overlooks information contained in the list length.

contributions.claim: Introduces and taxonomizes approaches for jointly modeling distributions over top-k partial orders and list lengths, including composite and augmented ranking models.
Defines three dependency structures for composite models and alternative assumptions for modeling stop-token choices in augmented ranking models.
Applies the models to partial rankings from San Francisco school choice and ranked choice elections.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The models were evaluated on partial-ranking data from San Francisco school choice and ranked choice elections for prediction and synthetic-data generation.
Composite models with categorical length modeling produced synthetic datasets with accurate length distributions.
An augmented model with position-dependent item utilities jointly modeled training-data length and preferences best by negative log loss.

narrative_sequence.summary: Agents submit partial orders over available alternatives in ranked-preference settings.
Marginal modeling through total orders can overlook information in the partial-order length.
The work compares composite truncation models and augmented ranking models with stop decisions, including variants within each class.
The models are evaluated on San Francisco partial-ranking data for observed-data prediction and synthetic-data generation.
Categorical length modeling improves synthetic length distributions, while a position-dependent augmented model achieves the best reported joint training-data fit by negative log loss.

source_observation.claim: Modeling list length explicitly can improve the realism of generated ranked-preference data.

interpretation.claim: The stopping or truncation process contains predictive information beyond the observed preference order.

application.claim: When simulating ranked preferences, evaluate and model both order structure and list-length distributions.

exception.claim: The reported findings are based on the cited San Francisco datasets and may not generalize to all ranked-preference settings.

unknowns: No quantitative results beyond the reported qualitative comparisons and negative-log-loss criterion are provided.
The abstract does not specify the model parameterizations, dependency structures, stop-token assumptions, or baseline details.
The abstract does not report dataset sizes, train-test procedures, or reproducibility information.
